{{More sources needed|date=May 2014}}

In the theory of [[algebraic group]]s, a '''special group''' is a [[linear algebraic group]] ''G'' with the property that every [[principal bundle|principal ''G''-bundle]] is locally trivial in the [[Zariski topology]].  Special groups include the [[general linear group]], the [[special linear group]], and the [[symplectic group]].  Special groups are necessarily [[Connected space|connected]].  Products of special groups are special. The [[projective linear group]] is not special because there exist [[Azumaya algebra]]s, which are trivial over a finite [[separable extension]], but not over the base field.

Special groups were defined in 1958 by [[Jean-Pierre Serre]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Serre |first=Jean-Pierre |date=1958 |title=Espaces fibrés algébriques |url=http://www.numdam.org/item/SCC_1958__3__A1_0/ |journal=Séminaire Claude Chevalley |language=French |volume=3 |via=Numdam}}</ref> and classified soon thereafter by [[Alexander Grothendieck]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Grothendieck |first=Alexander |date=1958 |title=Torsion homologique et sections rationnelles |url=http://www.numdam.org/item/SCC_1958__3__A5_0/ |journal=Séminaire Claude Chevalley |language=French |volume=3 |via=Numdam}}</ref>
